etymologies.etymologyHTML: Learned borrowing from Late Latin dēteriorātus, past participle of Late Latin dēteriorō, derivative of Latin dēterior (“worse”).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To make worse; to make inferior in quality or value; to impair.

quote.citation: 1829, Robert Southey, “(please specify the page)”, in Sir Thomas More: or, Colloquies on the Progress and Prospects of Society. […], volume (please specify |volume=I or II), London: John Murray, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: The art of war, like every other art, ecclesiastical architecture alone excepted, was greatly deteriorated during those years of general degradation […]

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To grow worse; to be impaired in quality; to degenerate.

quote.citation: 1947 January and February, O. S. Nock, “"The Aberdonian" in Wartime”, in Railway Magazine, page 7:
quote.text: During this fine run through Fife the weather had deteriorated rapidly, and as we passed Wormit and came onto the Tay Bridge heavy rain clouds were piled over the sea.

quote.citation: 2011 January 8, Paul Fletcher, “Stevenage 3 - 1 Newcastle”, in BBC‎[1]:
quote.text: It was turning into an abysmal afternoon for Newcastle and it deteriorated further when Tiote saw red for his challenge on Jon Ashton.
